Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "on 14 March at Alder Mill's dye room, the log has batch 24-031, an 18 kilogram cotton run for slate blue, at vat C2. the schedule had it down for a 7:10 start, but the dyeing did not start until 7:46. Leon Park was the operator on the morning shift, and Nia Soto was the maintenance technician assigned to the room. The delay was not because the shade recipe had been changed or because the cotton was missing. The rinse return valve strainer was packed with lint, so the return flow was too low for the rinse cycle to begin. That was the practical cause of the late start, and the log records it after the inspection rather than as an explanation guessed beforehand.

At 7:18, Leon noticed the flow indicator holding below its usual mark and stopped the preparation step. He did not put dye into the vat while the return line was restricted. Nia checked the line and opened the strainer housing; she found lint pressed against the screen. In her note she wrote, “The return is barely moving; the strainer is full of lint.” She removed the lint, rinsed the screen, and put the housing back in place. The indicator rose after she restored the flow, and Leon recorded that the rinse cycle could proceed. The maintenance note gives the cleaning as the reason the restriction was cleared; it does not describe a valve replacement or any change to the dye formula.

The batch record says Leon began the rinse at 7:46 and used the normal rinse sequence. It lists the same slate-blue recipe that had been prepared for the run before the delay, with no revised quantities entered. The cotton weighed 18 kilograms at the start, and the recorded vat was C2 throughout the operation. The log gives a rinse-water temperature of 31 degrees Celsius and a first dye addition at 8:12. Those times matter because the start time in the daily plan is not the same as the start time of the actual rinse. The form has separate boxes for planned start, actual start, and first dye addition, and Leon filled all three rather than putting the later time in the margin.

1. Morning entry and correction

The first copy of the daily sheet showed 7:10 in the actual-start box, although the handwritten batch notes beside it gave 7:46. Leon drew one line through 7:10, left the original number readable, and entered 7:46 beside it. He initialed that correction and wrote “strainer clean” in the reason field. He did not erase the planned time from the schedule column. Nia signed the maintenance entry at 7:34, after cleaning the screen and before Leon began the rinse. The two entries therefore put the inspection and cleaning before the recorded actual start, rather than making it look as though the maintenance work happened after the batch was already running. The paper copy stayed in the room until the afternoon review.

The rinse continued without another interruption, according to Leon's shift notes. At 8:12 he added the first dye portion, and at 8:26 he noted that the liquor had reached the logged circulation mark. The next entries list the second addition at 8:41 and the final hold beginning at 9:05. He wrote down each time as it happened, not as a single retrospective account at the end of the shift. The record does not say that the delayed start changed the shade, shortened the hold, or required extra dye. It says only that the batch followed the listed recipe and that the standard checks were entered at their usual points. I kept those statements separate from the cause of the delay when I copied the account into the weekly notebook.

I felt embarrassed when I saw how easily the planned time could be mistaken for the actual one on the first copy. I may have sounded impatient when I asked Leon why both times appeared on the page, but I cannot be certain how my voice came across. He showed me the correction and explained that the schedule time belonged in its own column. That answer helped me understand the form, though my reaction was still embarrassment rather than anger at Leon or Nia. Neither of them had entered a false time: the first figure had been written in the wrong box, then corrected with the original still visible. I noted my uncertainty about my tone separately from the log's factual explanation of the delay.

At the afternoon review, I compared the paper sheet with the room's shift notebook. The notebook also lists the low return flow, the lint at the strainer, and Nia's cleaning work, with the same times for the inspection and the start. It does not include a photograph of the screen, and no photograph was added to the paper file that day. The daily sheet was clipped behind the maintenance note, while the recipe card remained with the batch papers. This arrangement made it possible to read the operational record in sequence, but it did not make the planned start disappear; that time remained visible in the schedule column.

The final log entry records the vat as released from the room at 10:18, after the listed checks were complete. The page does not say that I approved the batch, and I did not add an approval mark when copying the times into the weekly notebook. I wrote the actual start as 7:46, retained 7:10 as the planned time, and noted that the strainer had been cleaned before the rinse began. The notebook's next line is a separate inventory entry for the afternoon shift, recording two unopened screen-cleaning brushes in the maintenance drawer.
